articles.title: Morelia Film Festival Prizes: ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building,’ an ‘Expression of Pure, Unbound Beauty,’ Wins Top ‘Ojo’ Award
articles.summary: Bruno Santamaría Razo’s fiction debut “Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”(“Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul”) has clinched the top Ojo award at the 24th Morelia Film Festival (FICM), which wraps Oct. 25.
body: Hailed by Variety as a “lush, poetic film rooted in memories,” it became the first Mexican feature to compete at Cannes’ Critics Week in 20 years.
Drawing on the filmmaker’s own experiences, the drama traces back to a defining moment in his childhood: the year he turned eleven and when his father was diagnosed with HIV.
“Six Months…” also nabbed the Audience Award for fiction films, a strong indication of its box office potential.

Alejandro Ramírez, Cinépolis CEO and FICM president, described the festival’s 24th edition as a particularly Mexican celebration as it welcomed some of Mexico’s finest filmmakers and actors, including Guillermo del Toro, Alfonso Cuarón, Carlos Reygadas, Jonás Cuarón, Diego Luna, Gael García Bernal, Demián Bichir, Diego Boneta and Luis Gerardo Méndez.

articles.title: Bill Murray Is Generally OK Giving You a “Bill Murray Moment”
articles.summary: "If you're living correctly, it's not a burden," Murray tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of his and Tom Coyne's new Paramount golf/travel series.
body: A Course Called Ireland, an adaptation of Coyne’s 2009 book of the same name, premieres Sunday on Paramount+. The six-episode, 30-minutes-per-episode series is as breezy as the Irish coast’s weather. Its original intention was to retrace the journey chronicled in Coyne’s bestseller — the golf writer once walked the island playing every golf course it had to offer — but this version of A Course Called Ireland became, as Murray grumpily laments in at least one episode to a director, “The Bill Murray Fucking Show.”
Murray has time for pretty much everyone who wants a photo — it is the production crew taking the professional videos he’d like to avert the lenses of.

“I’m heavy in the show. For an executive producer, that’s about as heavy as you can get,” Murray told The Hollywood Reporter. “I don’t want to complain about that. I did my complaining then. It’s too late to complain.”

I’m on a Zoom call with Murray, who is wandering the streets of Boston solo after sunset, and Coyne, who is sitting in a house in the Carribean. In a bucket hat and without a care in the world, Murray speaks kindly but candidly about making his buddy Coyne’s TV dream come true.

articles.title: Dark Matter Creator Doesn't Have 'Respect' For Marvel's Multiversal Storytelling [Exclusive]
articles.summary: Blake Crouch, who wrote Dark Matter and is the showrunner of the Apple TV adaptation, does not respect Marvel Studios' approach to multiversal storytelling.
body: There's just something appealing about the idea of the multiverse, as "Dark Matter" author and series creator Blake Crouch knows all too well. When he first published his heady sci-fi novel in 2016, it came at a time when pop culture had already become familiar with this subject matter (as any "Doctor Who" or "Star Trek" fan can attest to)... but before it took off to another level with the glut of superhero media throughout the last several years. "Avengers: Endgame" and its universe-hopping hijinks were still years away, as were blockbusters like "Spider-Man: No Way Home" and the very subtly-titled "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness."

The one commonality linking practically all of these various multiverse stories together, of course, is that writers mostly used this as an excuse to smash action figures together and revel in nostalgia. You love Spider-Man? How about a bunch of different Spider-Mans from different franchises! You loved Robert Downey Jr. as basically the main character of the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe? Good news, his (hilariously short-lived) retirement is done and he's back as Doctor Doom!
points: Blake Crouch, who wrote Dark Matter and is the showrunner of the Apple TV adaptation, does not respect Marvel Studios' approach to multiversal storytelling.

articles.title: Every Clayface Episode Of Batman: The Animated Series, Ranked
articles.summary: Long before Clayface made his debut on the big screen, he had one of the darkest villain arcs in Batman: The Animated Series.
body: DC Studios' "Clayface" owes a debt to "Batman: The Animated Series." The movie is a loose, feature-length remake of Clayface's first appearance on that show, the two-part episode "Feat of Clay." In that episode, actor Matt Hagen — left scarred by an accident — uses experimental chemicals to restore his movie star looks, but abuse of those chemicals turns him into a shapeshifting super-villain.

"Batman: The Animated Series" used Clayface rarely, but he's remembered as one of the show's most tragic villains, neck-and-neck with Mr. Freeze (Michael Ansara) and Two-Face (Richard Moll). When it's a Clayface episode, don't expect a happy ending. So let's look back at every time Clayface starred on "Batman: The Animated Series," as well as its sequel series/third season "The New Batman Adventures."

articles.title: Quentin Tarantino Shows Off First 17 Minutes of ‘Cliff Booth’ and Explains Decision to Revive Character
articles.summary: The director surprised AFI Fest with a first look at the follow-up, following a screening of 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.'
body: Before showing off the footage — which saw Booth working as a cinema projectionist while handling some more unsavory business on the side — Tarantino explained his decision to revisit the character in the first place.

“I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I kind of remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, it was like, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in,’ and there is that aspect,” he told the crowd. “I loved the Cliff Booth character, I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”

articles.title: Why John Borrelli From Clayface Looks So Familiar
articles.summary: John Borrelli seems to be the only honest cop in the Gotham Police Department in Clayface. Here's who plays the character.
body: It's been 7 years since the release of the very first feature film based entirely on a DC comics villain, with "Joker" going from a huge gamble to a monumental box office sensation. In the time since, we've had Marvel give a whole TV show to "Loki," Sony tried to build an entire cinematic universe based on "Spider-Man" villains that failed spectacularly, and DC gave Joker an underwhelming sequel and a more successful Penguin a TV show.

Now, we have "Clayface," the latest attempt to give a classic comic book villain his own feature film. /Film's review calls the film shapeless and forgettable, with its version of Gotham city indistinguishable from any other place. Though we never see Batman himself, the movie still very much feels like part of the Bat-universe, recognizable to anyone who has ever seen a story set in Gotham. This very much starts with the film's depiction of the world's worst police department, the Gotham City PD, which is as corrupt and inept as we've ever seen in a Batman-related movie.
